conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a brief, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days, and your answers stay between you and your care team. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to start?

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but if something’s genuinely funny I’ll smile or chuckle. It just feels like it takes a little more effort than it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, like I said, I can still laugh—just not quite as freely as before. Sometimes I’ll catch myself smiling at something silly my partner does or a funny show, but it feels kind of muted, like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy the moment.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes. I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk by myself—but mostly it feels flat. Planning anything fun just sounds exhausting right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like, the baby was extra fussy one night and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered him, or that I wasn’t soothing him right. Rationally I know babies just cry, but I still caught myself going, “What did I do wrong?”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days I do feel that knot in my stomach, even when everything looks fine on the outside. I’ll check that he’s breathing a hundred times, or worry that a tiny cough means he’s getting sick, even though there’s no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice I’ve had that sudden rush—like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath—but it passes pretty fast. It’s usually when the baby’s crying and I can’t settle him right away; for a minute it feels like everything’s spiraling, even though I know it’s not.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel like I’m drowning in little tasks. I usually manage, but it’s that constant “what’s next?” feeling—like I can’t quite get my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do have trouble falling asleep, but it’s more because my mind keeps running through the next feed or whether I sterilized the bottles right. I’m not lying there sobbing or anything—just wired and restless, especially the nights he’s had a rough day.
I have felt sad or miserable

Off and on. I’ll catch myself feeling heavy, like the color’s drained out of the day, but it’s not all day long. Sometimes when the baby finally settles and the house is quiet, I just sit there and feel… empty, I guess. It lifts after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I got a little teary one evening when my husband found me folding onesies and asked how I was doing, but actual crying—no, I haven’t broken down or anything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again.

You're doing your best in these early weeks of motherhood, yet it's clear the joy feels muted and the days often heavy. You shared that laughter comes less easily, excitement is fleeting, and a knot of worry sits in your stomach even when everything looks fine. Moments of feeling overwhelmed, self-blame when your baby is fussy, and that drained, empty sensation that keeps returning all point to how hard you're trying while feeling you're running on empty.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response indicates diminished enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure—still present occasionally but markedly reduced from baseline</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times this week" tied to specific incidents, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>She reports near-daily physical anxiety ("knot in the stomach") coupled with excessive, unfounded worries about the baby's breathing and health—clearly "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes triggered by infant distress, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent overwhelm ('some days, yeah') and feeling 'drowning in little tasks,' which aligns with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring sadness that comes and goes but is clearly present, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale falls above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. Key symptoms align with DSM-5 criteria: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>: "enjoyment feels flat"), depressed mood most days (<sym>low mood</sym>: "color drained out of the day"), inappropriate guilt (<sym>self-blame</sym>: "what did I do wrong?"), anxiety marked by near-daily physical tension and unfounded fears about infant health, and functional impact ("drowning in little tasks"). No self-harm thoughts were endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and consider therapy or medication options
2. Schedule within 1-2 weeks for re-screening and formal mental-health evaluation
3. Plan daily 15-minute self-care breaks (shower, short walk, quiet tea) while a trusted person watches baby
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when feeling panicky
5. Share these findings with your partner or support person so they can help monitor mood changes
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep hours, and anxiety episodes to review with your clinician
7. Contact local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities for peer support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
(Responses to EPDS-10 equivalents)

Symptoms / Concerns endorsed  
• Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh; enjoyment “flat” or “muted”  
• Persistent low mood: intermittent feelings of “empty,” “heavy,” “color drained”  
• Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
• Generalized anxiety: “knot in stomach,” repetitive worry about infant health  
• Situational panic symptoms: sudden racing heart/difficulty breathing when infant cries  
• Feeling overwhelmed / unable to “get head above water”  
• Initial insomnia related to ruminating about infant care  
• No crying spells; no self-harm ideation

Patterns / Risk indicators  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present daily, waxing/waning, without functional impairment in infant safety. Distress peaks with infant fussiness or accumulated tasks. No current safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Findings consistent with probable **postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety**; score approximates 10–11 on EPDS (above clinical cut-off of 9/10). Recommend follow-up assessment for formal diagnosis and discussion of psychosocial supports.
